term will be 1 September 2026 to 31 August 2030.

decision_maker: Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member for Safe and Genuinely Affordable Home
purpose:
This report seeks Cabinet Member
approval to undertake public consultation on a revised
Housing Allocations Policy for the borough, responding to
sustained pressure where demand continues to exceed supply and
ensuring alignment with statutory requirements, including the
Housing Act 1996 and Homelessness Reduction Act 2017, alongside
local need and operational priorities.  
 
The revised Policy will introduce a
more strategic approach to lettings, including a Local
Lettings Plan framework, stronger eligibility criteria,
clearer prioritisation, increased use of direct offers,
enhanced governance, and strengthened partnership working through
targeted allocation quotas for Adult and Children’s Services
in line with Care Act 2014 and Children Act
duties. 
These changes aim to ensure fair and
transparent allocations focused on those in greatest need, make
best use of limited housing stock, improve access to settled homes,
and reduce reliance on Temporary Accommodation, supporting the
council’s wider housing priorities.

value for money and programme efficiency.

procurement is carried out under the RE:FIT

Performance Contracting Framework Agreement
to appoint a delivery partner for the completion of
these works.

decision_maker: Strategic Director of Economy and Sustainability
purpose:
This report seeks approval to
award a contract for the demolition of the Phase 1 blocks (Colne,
Dee and Humber Courts) and the former community centre at High Lane
Estate, in line with Cabinet’s decision of July 2025 to
proceed with these enabling works. The buildings are currently
vacant, unsafe and deteriorating, creating ongoing public safety,
financial and reputational risks for the Council, as well as
undermining confidence in the wider regeneration
programme.
 
The decision requested will
enable the Council to remove these risks, eliminate recurring
holding and security costs, protect committed Greater London
Authority funding, and maintain momentum on the regeneration of the
estate. Demolition will also de-risk the site, improve its
condition and security, and enhance future land value while
longer-term development options for the wider estate are
progressed.

content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 

1.    
Approved the direct award of an interim contract to
Central London Community Healthcare Trust (CLCH) for a 15-month
period commencing from 1 October 2025 until 31 December 2026 (under
PSR option C) to enable the continued provision of the statutory
0-19 Healthy Child Programme (HCP) service whilst a new contract is
procured.
 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED
 

1.    
Direct Award of a bridging contract to the
current provider
This is the
most optimal option that allows officers time to prepare tenders to
the open market. The direct award will be for a period of 15 months
to enable the full tendering process to be undertaken.
RECOMMENDED OPTION.

 

2.    
Decommissioning the Service
This
is not an option as the council has a statutory responsibility to
provide the 0-19 Healthy Child Programme service under its public
health duties. NOT RECOMMENDED.
 

3.    
Competitive Process
Cabinet
authority has previously been obtained to commence a competitive
tendering process in order to have a new
contract in place on 1 January 2027. Two neighbouring boroughs have
also chosen to explore a competitive process for their 0-19
Services which provides additional options of future joint
procurement to maximise efficiencies and work collaboratively
across boroughs. Not Recommended for this 15-month period but
will be used for the future re-procurement.
 

4.    
Direct Award via PSR  
This was
explored but is no longer feasible due to budgetary constraints.
NOT RECOMMENDED.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the direct award of an interim contract to Central London Community Healthcare Trust for the 0-19 Healthy Child Programme service.

purpose:

budget proposals for the financial year 2026/27 and over the period

content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 
Revenue Budget
 
1.      
Approved total General Fund savings of £20.5m
over the MTFS period 2026/27 to 2029/30, of which £11.9m is
to be delivered from the General Fund in 2026/27 (Appendix
2).
 
2.      
Following full Council approval of each proposal,
authorises the Strategic Director with responsibility for each
proposal (including fees and charges) to:
a)          
carry out all necessary steps to implement each
proposal, including any necessary consultation.
b)          
consider any consultation outcomes and other
implications.
c)          
complete and consider the implications of any
equalities analysis assessment required.
d)          
following the above:
i)           
determine whether to amend any proposal
ii)          
determine whether a further report needs to be
considered by the relevant decision maker before
implementation
iii)         
where a decision is taken not to proceed, bring
forward alternative proposal(s).
             
                                                                  
3.      
Approved £30.4m of revenue growth for
pressures and investments in 2026/27 which will be included in
departmental control totals used for service budget
setting.
 
4.      
Noted the budget proposals are presented in advance
of the publication of the Final Local Government Finance
Settlement, and delegates any amendments
to the budget proposals as a result of
changes in the final settlement to the Strategic Director,
Resources in consultation with the Leader and the Cabinet Member
for Inclusive Economy.
 
 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 

1.      
The purpose of this report on the 2026/27 Budget and
Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) is to enable Cabinet to
consider the budget proposals and make recommendations to Full
Council when it finalises the budget and sets council tax on 3
March 2026.

2.      
The option not to consider the budget and council
tax proposals was not considered as the council is legally required
to set a balanced budget and council tax each financial
year.

3.      
The council has continued to provide budget growth
in services that experience significant and continued demand and
market pressures, with prioritisation being given to the most
vulnerable groups. Due to the complexity of the service provision
and notwithstanding the increase in cash-terms in funding in the
Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement, these services
continue to operate in a challenging resource environment where
even small demand changes can lead to material budget
variances.

4.      
The savings proposals in this report align with the
strategic vision, Council Plan and the MTFS on the allocation of
resources. Some of the savings proposals
may have further implications which will only emerge following
detailed planning and consultation. Where this is the case, those
implications will be considered before a final decision is taken on
implementation, including whether a proposal should be amended.
Where detailed proposals result in a lower financial saving, it is
the responsibility of the relevant Strategic Director to find
alternative replacement savings.

 

Cllr Mason on behalf of Cabinet, put on record his
thanks to officers for working together with the administration to
bring together a historic no-cuts budget the first in fifteen
years.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve £20.5m in General Fund savings over the 2026/27 to 2029/30 period, with £11.9m to be delivered in 2026/27.

purpose:
The Community-led Regeneration Charter (CRC)
is a non-statutory document co-developed between the council, the
community and other stakeholders involved in growth and
regeneration projects. Framed by the council’s Connected
Communities vision and the Community Charter (July 2025), the CRC's
principal purpose is to set out how communities can effectively and
meaningfully engage with and inform projects that are coming
forward within their towns and neighbourhoods, in order that their
unique needs are met and delivered by those leading the projects,
including the council and private developers. The CRC also clearly
defines the roles and responsibilities of all stakeholder's
involved in regeneration and growth projects and will be
accompanied by a toolkit for its practical application

RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 
1.  Approved the
Community-led Regeneration Charter in appendix 1.
 
2.  Delegated authority to the Strategic Director for
Economy & Sustainability to approve changes to the Charter and
the Engagement Toolkit that will be appended to the Charter,
following consultation with the Cabinet Member for Good Growth and
New Homes.
 

REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:

 
1.    
The Council’s Plan 2022–2026 sets out a
commitment to “Set out a new Community Led Regeneration
Charter.”
 
2.    
Evidence from past consultation feedback affirms
that good community engagement and a clear set of priorities is
essential to deliver good regeneration projects.
 
3.    
The council is actively working to tackle the
housing crisis across the borough. The Charter will be essential to
support with how the council, and its partners collaborate with the
community to deliver much needed affordable housing.
 
4.    
The Charter will bring greater consistency and
clarity in how Ealing’s local communities will be better
enabled to engage, inform, influence and shape regeneration
projects across the seven towns, with a focus on amplifying the
voices of the seldom heard and those who feel left
behind.
 
Option 1: Do
nothing 
 
5.    
Take no further action to publish the Community-led
Regeneration Charter.
 

Disadvantages: 
 
6.    
The council would fail to meet
its commitment under Ealing Council’s Plan 2022–2026,
which is to “Set out a new Community Led Regeneration
Charter”.
 
7.    
It would also damage trust with the community and
other stakeholders as a period of extensive engagement has been
undertaken.
 

Advantages: 
 
8.    
No further staff time would be required to advance
this project. 
 
Option 2: Approve the Community-led Regeneration Charter in
appendix 1 and the recommendations.
 

Disadvantages: 
 
9.    
None.
 

Advantages: 
 
10. 
The council meets its commitment under Ealing Council’s Plan 2022–2026,
which is to “Set out a new Community Led Regeneration
Charter.”
 
11. 
The council further strengthens and enhances
opportunities for communities to inform good growth and
regeneration projects in the borough.

purpose:
This report recommends the award of a building
contract to undertake ground risk mitigation and enabling works at
the Gurnell Leisure Centre site. This award forms part of a
two-stage tender process which has been undertaken in accordance
with the Council's contract procedure rules.
content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 
1.          
Agreed to enter
into a ground
risk mitigation and enabling works contract with Willmott Dixon
for works at the Gurnell Leisure Centre site.
 
 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 
1.    
The recommendation to instruct the ground risk
mitigation and enabling works package ahead of
entering
into the main
works contract is informed by risk management and cost efficiency.
The enabling works will address essential ground remediation and
site preparation, significantly reducing uncertainty around soil
conditions and associated cost risk before committing the Council
to the full construction contract. This approach also provides an
opportunity to partially offset inflationary pressures by
delivering works sooner than would be the case were these works
contained within the main contract.
 
2.    
In addition, commencing enabling works shortens the
overall programme by allowing preparatory activities to run ahead
of the main construction phase. While this requires an upfront
financial commitment, it is a necessary step to mitigate project
risks and prevent additional costs or delays in delivering the new
leisure centre.
 
3.    
The recommendation is proceed with a fixed-price enabling works package and defer
entering into the full main works
contract at this stage. This approach significantly reduces
financial exposure and contractual risk at this stage while
addressing critical site preparation, including ground remediation,
which is essential for de-risking the project. It also allows early
certainty on scope and costs before committing to the much larger
main works contract.
 
4.    
The alternative is to include the enabling works
within the main construction contract at a later stage, which would
require a large financial commitment without fully quantifying
ground conditions. This increases the risk of unforeseen costs and
programme delays. For these reasons, the enabling works option is
considered the most prudent and cost-effective route
forward.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to enter into a ground risk mitigation and enabling works contract with Willmott Dixon for works at the Gurnell Leisure Centre site.

purpose:
The project will procure a 24/7 high-need
supported housing service with integrated housing management for
men aged 18+ with complex, diagnosed mental health needs who are
homeless or at risk of homelessness. One contract will deliver both
the support services and the housing management.
content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 

Agreed to run an open
tender to procure a supported housing service at Dame Gertrude
House for men aged 18 and over with complex mental health needs who
are homeless or at risk of homelessness for three years with the
option to extend for up to two additional years in one-year
intervals.

 

Delegated authority
to the Strategic Director of Housing and Environment to award the
contract. 

 

Delegated authority
to the Strategic Director of Housing and Environment to exercise
the options to extend the contract.

 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 

1.      
The decision is required to ensure continuity of a
critical service for men with complex mental health needs who are
homeless or at risk of homelessness. The expiry of the previous
contracts, combined with the need to maintain a robust 24/7 support
model, makes procurement of a new integrated contract
essential.

 

2.      
The preferred single contract approach delivers best
value by improving accountability, reducing duplication, and
enabling the council to review operational efficiencies over the
lifetime of the contract, including safe adjustments to night-time
staffing.

 
 The following options were assessed
when determining the recommended approach:
 
        
I.       
Do nothing - Rejected due to high safeguarding,
financial, and statutory risks.
      
II.       
Separate contracts for housing management and
support - Rejected due to fragmentation, higher costs, and reduced
accountability.
    
III.       
Housing Management to manage the building and
support by a contractor - Rejected due to fragmentation and reduced
accountability
    
IV.       
Single integrated contract – Preferred option
as it delivers best value, improved outcomes, service
continuity.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to procure a supported housing service at Dame Gertrude House for men with complex mental health needs who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.

purpose:
This report outlines the new approach to
enforcing the parking of dockless e-bikes in the borough.
content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 
1.         
Approved the E-Bike Enforcement Procedure at
Appendix 1;
2.          
Agreed to the implementation of the E-Bike
Enforcement Procedure for a six-month pilot period; and
3.          
Delegated authority to the Strategic Director,
Housing & Environment to continue the E-Bike Enforcement
Procedure following the pilot period.
 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 
1.    
An e-bike enforcement policy is a useful tool to
protect the council from obstructive incursions by an e-bike
operator without an agreement in place, as well as to build upon
provisions in current MoUs which
stipulate good parking practices. The formalised procedure to
enforce against obstructively parked e-bikes will respond to recent
resident feedback, address accessibility concerns, and
support the council’s policy to require
mandatory parking in ‘virtual’ or ‘marked’
bays. Enforcement has been successfully
implemented by other London boroughs in the absence of pan-London
micromobility licensing.
 
2.    
The option of maintaining the status quo (asking and
expecting operators with MoUs to
continue to manage e-bike parking) was considered, but this could
not apply to operators without an MoU and is not considered
sufficient to address the observed issues and complaints related to
obstructive parking and bay capacity.
 
3.    
Maintaining current practice and enforcing only
against unpermitted operators who do not have an agreement with the
council was also considered; however, this would not address
obstructive parking from e-bikes of permitted operators.
 
4.    
Maintaining current practice and allowing
unpermitted operators to retain access to the borough, with certain
conditions such as a small fleet cap of 200 e-bikes, is also not
recommended. It would still be difficult to
enforce the conditions set by the council, without an agreement or
enforcement policy, and this would increase the number of bikes in
the current operating area, thereby increasing parking
pressure.
 
5.    
The recommended approach of publishing and trialling
an enforcement procedure that covers mis-parked and obstructive
e-bikes of all operators (alongside a pragmatic approach of
allowing ‘ride-throughs’ and a review of borough
boundary parking) is deemed to be a balanced approach to address
observed parking issues and maintain collaborative relationships
with micromobility operators.
 
6.    
A drawback of introducing this enforcement policy is
that it places the onus for micromobility asset management upon the
council, when this responsibility should lie with the operators and
their management of their own assets. However, in the
circumstances, the council believes the benefits of enforcement
outweigh this drawback.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve and implement an E-Bike Enforcement Procedure for a six-month pilot period.

content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 
1.          
Agreed that Appendices 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 are not for
publication on the basis that they contain information relating to
the financial or business affairs of any particular person (including the authority holding
that information) as set out in paragraph 3 of Schedule 12A of the
Local Government Act 1972 (as amended).
 

2.          
Agreed to enter into a development agreement (DA)
and development lease (based on the drafts at Appendix 2 and 3)
with Countryside Properties (UK) Limited (the development lease to
be executed only once the conditions precedent outlined in the DA
have been met).
 

3.          
Agreed to transfer the freehold in accordance with
the terms of the DA.
 

4.          
Delegated authority to the Strategic Director for
Economy and Sustainability to appropriate the site for planning
purposes at the relevant time.
 

5.          
Delegated authority to the Strategic Director
Economy and Sustainability to agree the final versions of the DA
and development lease, enter into all
ancillary legal documents required and take all necessary steps to
facilitate the project or protect the council’s
interests.
 
 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 
 
1.          
The residential development is, defined in planning
terms as, enabling development for new leisure centre as it will
provide a capital receipt to support the funding for the new
leisure centre. The funding for the new leisure centre will be the
subject of a future cabinet report.
 
2.          
In addition, the residential development will
provide much needed housing in the borough and will assist towards
meeting the borough’s housing target as set by the Greater
London Authority (GLA).
 
3.          
Following the conclusion of the full tender process,
the council’s procurement specialist (Savills) has prepared
the tender report at Appendix 1. Consequently, the recommendations
in this report have been prepared in line with the tender
report’s outcome.
 
4.          
The DA will give the council control over the
delivery on the site, without the risks associated with direct
delivery, and whilst still generating a capital receipt for use as
capital subsidy for the new leisure centre.
 
 
 
Not to award
the contract for disposal of the site
 
5.          
This would create a financial risk, as the council
would be unable to recoup its direct costs incurred during the
tender and pre-tender processes (including legal, procurement,
design and planning fees).
 
6.          
This would also create a reputational risk for the
council as such a decision would contradict previous decisions made
by Cabinet.
 
To award the contract for disposal of the
site
 
7.          
This contract will generate a capital receipt to be
used to enable the development of the new Gurnell leisure
centre.

purpose:

for the Villiers High School new building main works project.
Authority to add funds to the capital programme.
content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 

1.    
Agrees that Appendix 1 is not for publication on the
basis that it contains information relating to the financial or
business affairs of any particular
person (including the authority holding that information) as
set out in paragraph 3 of Schedule 12A of the Local Government Act
1972 (as amended).
 

2.    
Agrees to increase the existing Villiers School
capital budget of £26.722m to £29.320m to reflect the
total costs of the works. and notes that the additional
£2.597m will be funded from grant, reserves and a
contribution from the school.
 

3.    
Agrees to award a contract to Morgan Sindall
Construction & Infrastructure Limited for the Villiers High
School Places construction works, funded from the revised Villiers
High School works capital budget of £29.320m.
 
REASONS FOR
DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 
1.      
The decision is required to enable the council to
progress with capital works to the school.
 
2.      
Under the council’s Constitution, Cabinet
approval is required to proceed with schemes over £5m per
annum in value, Portfolio Holder approval is required to proceed
with schemes between £0.500m and £5m per annum, and the
schemes up to £0.500m per annum fall within Director
delegated powers.

 
3.      
In September 2024, Cabinet authorised inviting and
evaluating tenders, or making call offs
from appropriate frameworks or dynamic purchasing systems, for the
pre-construction services agreement and works contracts required
for the Villiers High School Places project from the existing
approved capital programme budget for Villiers High
School.

 
4.      
In September 2024, Cabinet also delegated authority
to the Strategic Director, Children’s Services, to take all
necessary steps to award the pre-construction services agreement
and works contracts, such authority to include finalising,
negotiating and entering into all relevant ancillary legal
agreements.

 
5.      
The contract has been procured through the Southern
Construction Framework Agreement (SCF) - Lot 3 London. Contractor
selection was by Mini Competition to provide pre-construction
services on a fee basis, to then develop Contractor’s
Proposals during the pre-construction period.

 
6.      
In May 2025, the Strategic Director,
Children’s Services, approved the contractor appointment for
the pre-construction services agreement. The pre-construction
services activities have now been completed and the
Contractor’s Proposals including costs have been evaluated by
the council’s Projects Delivery Unit. 
 
7.      
This decision relates to the contractor appointment
for the main construction works contract at Villiers High
School.
 
8.      
A full range of options for the works required was
considered. These included: 
 
1)    
Do nothing.
2)    
Prolonging the timescale for replacement of the
existing block with the school continuing to repair and maintain,
and the council replace, systems and fabric elements.
3)    
Proceeding with the replacement of the existing
block with a larger block in isolation to attend to a shortfall of
space against pupil numbers.
4)    
Proceeding with replacement of the existing block in
tandem with additional accommodation for 1 form of entry (FE) and
enabling a Specialist Resourced Provision to follow.

 
9.      
In September 2024, Cabinet approved proceeding with
Option 4 and approved plans to invite and evaluate tenders, or make call offs from appropriate
frameworks or dynamic purchasing systems, for the pre-construction
services and works contracts required for the project.

 
10.   
Cabinet is now recommended to award a contract
to Morgan Sindall Construction &
Infrastructure Limited for the works
associated with Option 4.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to increase the capital budget for Villiers School and award a construction contract to Morgan Sindall Construction & Infrastructure Limited.

content:
RESOLVED:
 
That Cabinet:
 
I. Agreed to procure a contract
for the provision of the 0-19 Healthy Child
Programme (HCP) service via a
competitive process for an initial period of 4
years, with the option to
extend for a further 2 plus 1 years (7 years in total).
 
II. Delegated authority to the
Strategic Director for Children’s Services to award the
contract and exercise the option to extend.
 
 
REASONS FOR DECISION AND OPTIONS CONSIDERED:
 
1.  
Detailed contract negotiations which commenced in January 2025 have
now halted as the pricing now requested by the current provider
exceeds the current financial envelope available, despite
additional service investment from the council. 2.. A direct award
under the PSR (route C) is no longer permissible to the existing
provider due to the material change in the financial envelope.

 
2.  
A direct award under the PSR (route C) is no longer permissible to
the existing provider due to the material change in the financial
envelope.
 
3.  
The pricing requested by the existing provider will not facilitate
any future flexibilities in service design to meet ongoing demand
as the pricing reflects the service as it currently stands with
some further reduction to the Health Visiting Service.
 
4.  
Anecdotal evidence suggests NHS Trusts, may be increasing contract
costs to reduce deficits, potentially necessitating increased
funding regardless of contract status.
 
5.  
It is recommended that we prepare to carry out a competitive
process to secure value for money and explore alternative service
delivery models. Options include joint procurement with other local
authorities to maximise efficiencies.
 
6.  
Direct Award under PSR to current provider
 
7.  
The PSR has introduced four direct award processes that relevant
authorities can use to directly award contracts for health care
services. These are as follows:
 
a. the existing
provider is the only provider that can deliver the health care
services (direct award process A)
b. patients have a
choice of providers, and the number of providers is not restricted
by the relevant authority (direct award process B)
c. the existing
provider is satisfying its existing contract, will likely satisfy
the new contract to a sufficient standard, and the proposed
contracting arrangements are not changing considerably (direct
award process C).
d. The relevant
authority is not required to follow direct award process A or B,
the relevant authority cannot and does not wish to follow direct
award process C, the relevant authority is of the view (taking into
account likely providers and all relevant information available to
the relevant authority at the time), that it is likely to be able
to identify the most suitable provider (the most suitable provider
process)
 
• Direct award process C can be applied
when the current provider is performing well, and change would
negatively impact on the current service delivery model and risk an
increase in costs. However, restrictions under this direct award
option limit the ability to make material contract changes, thus
constraining financial and service design flexibility. NOT
RECOMMENDED
 
8.  Decommissioning
the Service 
This is not an option as council has a
statutory responsibility to provide the 0-19 Healthy Child
Programme service under its public health duties. NOT
RECOMMENDED
 
9. Direct Award via PSR – We have
explored partnering with other NHS Trusts through PSR, which could
shorten procurement times, strengthen established partnerships, and
lower management costs. However, since initial costings obtained
indicate this would require an investment of over 10% of the
contract value, this option restricts market testing which may not
deliver optimal value for money. NOT RECOMMENDED
 
10. Competitive Process
The current market is a limited market, and
there are challenges in the recruitment and retention of Health
Visiting and School Nursing regionally and nationally. The
programme includes mandated and non-mandated elements, with FNP and
MESCH being non-mandated but critical to Early Help and the Think
Family Approach. Carrying out a competitive process will help to
facilitate new ways of working with more flexible service delivery
options.
 
11. Two neighbouring boroughs have also chosen
to explore a competitive process for their 0-19 Services which
provides additional options of future joint procurement to maximise
efficiencies and work collaboratively across boroughs.
 
12. It was recommended that we prepare for an
open competitive process to secure value for money and explore
alternative innovative service delivery models to meet the changing
needs of the population. Options include joint procurement with
other local authorities to maximize efficiencies. RECOMMENDED
 
 

Decision subject to call-in
topline: The Cabinet has decided to procure a contract for the 0-19 Healthy Child Programme service via a competitive process.

purpose:
The Neutral Vendor Service (NVS) provider
contract provides a fast, cost-efficient way to procure low-value
contracts, enabling council to focus its limited resources on the
procurement of larger spend contracts.
 
The main purpose of the contract is to improve
process efficiency associated with sourcing and onboarding of
suppliers, encourage engagement of Small Medium Enterprises (SMEs)
and leverage economies of scale. This is achieved through the
management of end-to-end sourcing, supplier onboarding and payment
of low value contracts.
 
The NVS contract was awarded in 2021 for 4
years with optional 2-year extensions and has exceeded its primary
objectives. The contract is accessible to and is being used by
several other public sector organisations and continues to provide
an efficient market solution during a period of change and resource
pressures.
